q: Element X reacts with cold water more violently than potassium does. Where is X most likely to be in the Periodic Table?
explain: Reactivity of Group I metals increases down the group, so X is a Group I metal below potassium.

q: A balloon is filled with helium. Which property of helium makes it suitable?
options: It is reactive and denser than air.
It is unreactive and denser than air.
It is unreactive and less dense than air.
It is flammable and less dense than air.
explain: Helium is unreactive, so it is safe, and it has a lower density than air so the balloon rises.

q: Potassium has a relative atomic mass of 39. What volume of hydrogen at r.t.p. is made when 0.39 g of potassium reacts completely with water? (1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.)
Which pair of elements is in the same period of the Periodic Table?
explain: Sodium and chlorine both have three occupied shells (Period 3); the other pairs are in the same group.

q: What is the oxidation number of iron in Fe₂O₃?
explain: Three O²⁻ give a total of 6−, so each of the two iron atoms must be +3.

q: Reactivity of the halogens decreases down Group VII. Which halogen is the most reactive?
explain: Reactivity decreases down Group VII, so chlorine, at the top of this list, is the most reactive.

q: 0.10 mol of chlorine reacts with excess aqueous potassium bromide. What mass of bromine (relative molecular mass 160) is formed?
explain: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ gives 0.10 mol Br₂, and 0.10 × 160 = 16 g.

q: The densities of three noble gases at r.t.p. are: helium 0.17 g/dm³, neon 0.84 g/dm³, argon 1.66 g/dm³. Which is the most likely density of krypton?
explain: Density rises down the group, so krypton, below argon, must be greater than 1.66 g/dm³.

q: The boiling points of three halogens are: chlorine −35 °C, bromine 59 °C, iodine 184 °C. Which is the most likely boiling point of astatine?
explain: Boiling points rise down Group VII, so astatine, below iodine, should be above 184 °C.

q: What is the appearance of bromine at r.t.p.?
explain: Bromine is a red-brown liquid at r.t.p.; chlorine is a gas and iodine is a solid.

q: Caesium is in Group I below rubidium. Which property is it most likely to have compared with potassium?
explain: Melting points decrease down Group I, so caesium melts at a lower temperature than potassium.

q: Which statement about the positions of metals and non-metals in the Periodic Table is correct?
options: Metals are mainly on the right; non-metals are mainly on the left.
Metals are found only in the centre; non-metals are found only at the edges.
Metals are mainly on the left and in the centre; non-metals are mainly on the right.
Metals and non-metals are mixed evenly across every period.
explain: Metallic character is strongest on the left and in the centre, and non-metals are grouped towards the right.

q: Which row correctly describes chlorine, bromine and iodine at r.t.p.?
explain: Chlorine is a gas, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid, so the state changes down the group.

q: Astatine is below iodine in Group VII. Which property is it most likely to have?
explain: Halogens get darker and denser down the group, so astatine is a dark solid.

q: Compared with Group I metals, transition elements are generally
explain: Transition metals are hard and strong with high densities, unlike soft, low-density Group I metals.

q: Why are the noble gases unreactive?
options: Their atoms have a single outer electron.
Their atoms are very large and heavy.
Their atoms have full outer shells of electrons.
explain: A full outer shell is stable, so noble gas atoms do not need to gain, lose or share electrons.

q: How many electrons does a chlorine atom gain to form a chloride ion?
explain: A chlorine atom has 7 outer electrons and gains one electron to complete its outer shell.

q: Which row correctly describes chlorine and argon at r.t.p.?
explain: Chlorine exists as Cl₂ molecules, whereas argon is monatomic and exists as single atoms.

q: Which equation correctly shows lithium reacting with water?
explain: The balanced equation has two Li, four H and two O on each side, with LiOH as the alkali.

q: A Group I metal M is predicted to react with chlorine. Which equation is correct?
explain: M forms M⁺ ions, so the product is MCl; two atoms of M are needed for one Cl₂ molecule.

q: Potassium is added to water. Which observation is correct?
options: It sinks to the bottom and fizzes slowly.
It stays still and slowly dissolves.
It floats and burns with a red flame.
It moves quickly on the surface and burns with a lilac flame.
explain: Potassium reacts vigorously, melts and the hydrogen produced burns with a lilac flame.

q: Which equation shows chlorine displacing bromine from aqueous potassium bromide?
explain: Two bromide ions must be displaced to form one Br₂ molecule, so the equation needs 2KBr and 2KCl.

q: Which ionic equation represents the reaction of chlorine with aqueous potassium iodide?
explain: Potassium ions are spectators. The halide ions are exchanged and the charges balance on both sides.

q: Which row correctly names the horizontal rows and the vertical columns of the Periodic Table?
explain: Horizontal rows are called periods and vertical columns are called groups.

q: Sodium reacts with water to give sodium hydroxide. When all of 2.3 g of sodium (Aᵣ = 23) is used to make 1.0 dm³ of solution, what is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide?
explain: 2.3 g is 0.10 mol Na, which gives 0.10 mol NaOH in 1.0 dm³, so the concentration is 0.10 mol/dm³.

q: Manganese(IV) oxide is added to hydrogen peroxide solution. Oxygen is released rapidly. Which statement is correct?
options: The manganese(IV) oxide acts as a catalyst.
The manganese(IV) oxide is the reactant that makes oxygen.
The manganese(IV) oxide is permanently used up.
The manganese(IV) oxide acts as an oxidising agent only.
explain: Manganese(IV) oxide speeds up the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide and is unchanged at the end.

q: Iron is used in the Haber process to speed up the reaction without being used up. What is iron acting as?
explain: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction and is not used up, and transition elements often act as catalysts.

q: How does the density of the halogens change down Group VII?
explain: The density increases down the group, as shown by the change from gas to liquid to solid.

q: In the Periodic Table the elements are arranged in order of increasing
explain: The modern Periodic Table is ordered by proton (atomic) number, the number of protons in the nucleus.

q: How does the colour of the halogens change down the group?
options: It changes from dark to pale and back.
explain: The colours go from pale yellow-green to red-brown to grey-black, getting darker.
